subject: physics
pattern: Nuclei normally carries 6-8 marks: 1-mark definitions (isotopes, half-life, mass defect), a 2-mark question on nuclear force or decay equations, a 3-mark numerical on binding energy or half-life, and a 5-mark question on the radioactive decay law or the nuclear reactor. Examiners expect $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$, $T_{1/2} = 0.693/\lambda$, the binding energy curve and the use of 1 u = 931.5 MeV.

questions.q: What are isotopes? Give an example.
questions.answer: Isotopes are atoms of the same element having the same atomic number $Z$ (same number of protons) but different mass numbers $A$ (different number of neutrons). Example: hydrogen has the isotopes protium $\,{}^{1}_{1}$H, deuterium $\,{}^{2}_{1}$H and tritium $\,{}^{3}_{1}$H.

questions.q: Define half-life of a radioactive substance.
questions.answer: The half-life $T_{1/2}$ is the time taken for half of the radioactive nuclei present in a sample to decay (for the activity to fall to half its initial value). $T_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}$, where $\lambda$ is the decay constant.

questions.q: What is mass defect? Write the expression for the binding energy of a nucleus.
questions.answer: Mass defect is the difference between the sum of the masses of the free nucleons and the actual mass of the nucleus: $\Delta m = [Zm_p + (A-Z)m_n] - M$. Binding energy $E_b = \Delta m\,c^2$ (with 1 u $= 931.5$ MeV/$c^2$).
keywords: sum of nucleon masses minus nuclear mass

questions.q: Mention two properties of nuclear force.
questions.answer:
1. Nuclear force is a strong, short-range attractive force (effective up to about 2-3 fm); it is much stronger than electrostatic or gravitational force.
2. It is charge independent (the same between p-p, n-n and p-n) and saturated, so a nucleon interacts only with its neighbours; it is non-central and spin dependent. It becomes repulsive at distances less than about 0.8 fm.

questions.q: Write the expression for the radius of a nucleus. Show that nuclear density is independent of mass number.
questions.answer:
$R = R_0A^{1/3}$, where $R_0 = 1.2$ fm $= 1.2\times10^{-15}$ m.
Volume $V = \dfrac43\pi R^3 = \dfrac43\pi R_0^3A$ and mass $\approx A$ u, so density $\rho = \dfrac{A\,\mathrm{u}}{\frac43\pi R_0^3A} = \dfrac{\mathrm{u}}{\frac43\pi R_0^3}$, independent of $A$. Its value is about $2.3\times10^{17}$ kg m$^{-3}$.

questions.q: The half-life of a radioactive element is 8 years. What fraction of the initial amount will remain after 24 years?
questions.answer:
Number of half-lives $n = \dfrac{t}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{24}{8} = 3$.
$\dfrac{N}{N_0} = \left(\dfrac12\right)^n = \left(\dfrac12\right)^3 = \dfrac18$.
So 1/8 (12.5 per cent) of the initial amount remains.

questions.q: Write the nuclear reactions for (i) alpha decay of $\,{}^{238}_{92}$U and (ii) beta minus decay of $\,{}^{32}_{15}$P.
questions.answer:
(i) Alpha decay: $\,{}^{238}_{92}\mathrm{U} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{90}\mathrm{Th} + {}^{4}_{2}\mathrm{He}$ (mass number falls by 4, atomic number by 2).
(ii) Beta minus decay: $\,{}^{32}_{15}\mathrm{P} \rightarrow {}^{32}_{16}\mathrm{S} + e^- + \bar{\nu}$ (a neutron changes to a proton, atomic number rises by 1, mass number unchanged; an antineutrino is also emitted).

questions.q: The mass defect of a nucleus is 0.03 u. Calculate its binding energy in MeV. If the nucleus has 12 nucleons, find the binding energy per nucleon. (1 u = 931.5 MeV)
questions.answer:
$E_b = \Delta m \times 931.5$ MeV $= 0.03\times931.5 = 27.9$ MeV (27.945 MeV).
Binding energy per nucleon $= \dfrac{E_b}{A} = \dfrac{27.945}{12} = 2.33$ MeV per nucleon.

questions.q: Draw the graph of binding energy per nucleon against mass number and mention its important features.
questions.answer:
[Graph: rises steeply for light nuclei, has a broad maximum of about 8.75 MeV near $A\approx56$ (iron), then decreases slowly to about 7.6 MeV at $A\approx238$.]
Features: (i) the curve is nearly flat between $A = 30$ and $A = 170$ with an average of about 8 MeV per nucleon, so the force is saturated; (ii) it is maximum for iron-like nuclei, which are the most stable; (iii) light nuclei ($A<30$) have low binding energy per nucleon, so fusion of them releases energy; (iv) heavy nuclei ($A>170$) have lower values, so fission of them releases energy.

questions.q: Distinguish between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion (any three points).
questions.answer:
Fission: a heavy nucleus (e.g. U-235) splits into two lighter nuclei on neutron bombardment; it occurs at ordinary temperature; energy released is about 200 MeV per fission; it can be controlled in a reactor; the by-products are radioactive.
Fusion: two light nuclei (e.g. deuterium) combine to form a heavier nucleus; it needs a very high temperature ($\sim10^7$ K) to overcome Coulomb repulsion; energy per nucleon released is greater (about 3.3 MeV in D-D); it is difficult to control and is the source of solar energy; products are less hazardous.

questions.q: Show that the half-life of a radioactive substance is $T_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}$. Define mean life and write its relation with the decay constant.
questions.answer:
From the decay law, $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$. When $t = T_{1/2}$, $N = \dfrac{N_0}{2}$:
$\dfrac{N_0}{2} = N_0e^{-\lambda T_{1/2}} \Rightarrow e^{\lambda T_{1/2}} = 2 \Rightarrow \lambda T_{1/2} = \ln2 = 0.693$
$T_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda}$.
Mean life $\tau$ is the average time for which a nucleus survives, i.e. the sum of lifetimes of all nuclei divided by their number. $\tau = \dfrac{1}{\lambda}$, so $T_{1/2} = 0.693\,\tau$.

questions.q: State the law of radioactive decay and derive the expression $N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$.
questions.answer:
Law: the rate of decay of radioactive nuclei at any instant is directly proportional to the number of undecayed nuclei present at that instant.
Let $N$ be the number of nuclei at time $t$. Then $-\dfrac{dN}{dt} \propto N$, i.e. $-\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N$, where $\lambda$ is the decay constant (the minus sign shows that $N$ decreases).
Rearranging, $\dfrac{dN}{N} = -\lambda\,dt$.
Integrating, $\ln N = -\lambda t + C$. At $t = 0$, $N = N_0$, so $C = \ln N_0$.
$\ln\dfrac{N}{N_0} = -\lambda t \Rightarrow N = N_0e^{-\lambda t}$.
The activity $R = -\dfrac{dN}{dt} = \lambda N = R_0e^{-\lambda t}$ decays exponentially, SI unit becquerel (1 Bq = 1 decay per second).

questions.q: Explain nuclear fission and chain reaction. Describe the working of a nuclear reactor, mentioning the function of the moderator, control rods and coolant.
questions.answer:
Fission: a slow neutron strikes $\,{}^{235}_{92}$U, which splits into two medium-mass nuclei with 2-3 neutrons and about 200 MeV energy, e.g. $\,{}^{235}_{92}\mathrm{U} + {}^{1}_{0}n \rightarrow {}^{141}_{56}\mathrm{Ba} + {}^{92}_{36}\mathrm{Kr} + 3\,{}^{1}_{0}n + Q$. The emitted neutrons cause further fissions: a chain reaction.
Reactor: a controlled chain reaction takes place in fuel rods (enriched uranium).
- Moderator (heavy water or graphite) slows the fast neutrons to thermal energies so they can cause fission.
- Control rods (cadmium or boron) absorb excess neutrons and keep the multiplication factor $k = 1$.
- Coolant (water or liquid sodium) carries away heat to a heat exchanger, which makes steam to run turbines and generate electricity.
- Shielding (thick concrete) absorbs radiation.
